opus-5.5.text:
I think you have to be quite careful with it, because there's a seductive line of reasoning that goes: mathematics is the pinnacle of human intellectual achievement, the thing we associate with the very brightest people, so if AI systems are now solving olympiad problems or helping prove research-level results, they must be close to mastering everything else. I don't think that follows nearly as cleanly as it seems.

Part of the reason is that mathematics has some unusual features that make it especially amenable to the current approach. Above all, it's verifiable. In formal theorem proving, you can check whether a proof is correct mechanically, and even in informal maths there's often a crisp answer. That gives you an extraordinarily clean training signal. You can have a system generate enormous numbers of attempts, keep the ones that work, and learn from them, a kind of self-play. That's the same structure that let systems like AlphaGo go from human-level to superhuman, and it's no coincidence that the domains where we've seen the most dramatic recent jumps are mathematics and competitive programming, where you can check the answers.

Most of the intellectual tasks we care about don't look like that. Think about deciding on good policy, running a research programme, writing a really insightful essay, or even judging which mathematical questions are worth asking. There's no oracle that tells you, quickly and cheaply, whether you got it right. Feedback is slow, noisy, contested, sometimes only arrives years later. So the very thing powering progress in theorem proving is largely absent elsewhere.

There's also the point that benchmarks measure what's measurable. A competition problem is self-contained, with a known solution and a fixed time horizon. Real intellectual work is long-horizon and open-ended: you have to figure out what the problem even is, keep track of a project over weeks or months, notice when you've gone down a blind alley. I'd want to know not just whether a system can solve a hard problem, but how long a task it can carry through reliably, and how that horizon is growing.

That said, I don't want to dismiss it. There are a couple of ways it's genuine evidence. First, it shows these systems aren't merely pattern-matching on shallow features. Solving novel hard problems requires something we'd ordinarily call reasoning, and the skeptical position that they can never do that has taken a real hit. Second, mathematics and programming are themselves inputs to AI research. If systems become very capable in exactly the verifiable, technical domains that matter for building better AI, that could speed up progress in a way that matters a lot even if they remain patchy elsewhere.

So my overall take is that theorem-proving progress is strong evidence about what this paradigm can do when it has a good verifier, and weaker evidence about general intellectual mastery. The key question is how much of the rest of intellectual life can be turned into something verifiable, or whether skills learned in verifiable domains generalise to unverifiable ones. That's an empirical question we're watching unfold in real time, and I think intellectual honesty requires holding fairly wide uncertainty about it rather than reading the maths results as either "nearly there" or "just a parlour trick."

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes theorem proving from judging which mathematical questions are worth asking, but does not clearly state that AI could master theorem proving while still lacking that ability.

r002.rationale: It discusses the difficulty of judging which questions are worth asking, but does not address inventing new fields or the stated contrast.

r003.rationale: It cites AlphaGo and progress in verifiable domains, but does not describe a repeated pattern of mastering tasks once taken as evidence of general competence without attaining broader competence.

r004.rationale: It calls for measuring task horizons and expresses uncertainty, but does not note that few attempts systematically establish how little remains before broad intellectual mastery.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's genuinely impressive, and I also think it's one of the easier places to be fooled, so let me try to hold both of those at once.

The impressive part is real. A few years ago, if you'd told me that systems would be getting gold-medal-level results on International Mathematical Olympiad problems, or proving non-trivial results in a formal language like Lean, I'd have said that was a long way off. These are problems where you can't bluff. You can't produce a plausible-sounding paragraph and have it marked correct. Either the proof checks or it doesn't. So in that sense it's some of the cleanest evidence we have that these systems can do sustained, multi-step reasoning rather than just pattern-matching to the surface of a question.

But I'd be cautious about reading it as a straightforward signal of how close we are to mastering intellectual work in general, for a few reasons.

The first is that theorem-proving has a property that almost nothing else in intellectual life has, which is a perfect verifier. You can generate a million candidate proofs, check every one of them automatically, and train on the ones that worked. That's an extraordinarily favourable regime for the current methods. Most of what we'd want AI to do, whether that's writing good policy, running a scientific research programme, or making a judgement call about a messy situation, doesn't come with a referee that says yes or no in milliseconds. So progress in mathematics may be telling us about the ceiling of these systems when the feedback loop is ideal, rather than about the typical case.

The second is that the benchmarks are, by construction, problems with known answers. Competition mathematics is beautiful, but it's a curated world of problems that are designed to be solvable in a few hours by a clever teenager. Research mathematics is different in kind. It's about deciding which questions are worth asking, noticing that two fields are secretly the same, spending three years on something that may not pan out. I don't think we've yet seen strong evidence of that kind of taste and direction-setting, and I'd want to see it before I updated too hard.

The third thing I'd say, and this is more about how I think about forecasting generally, is that we've had a long history of picking a task that seems to require deep intelligence, watching a machine do it, and then quietly deciding it didn't require intelligence after all. Chess was the paradigm case. I don't want to make the opposite mistake, where I say that because mathematics feels like the pinnacle of thought, cracking it means everything else falls immediately. Capabilities have come in a jagged way. Systems that are superhuman at one thing can be strangely weak at something adjacent.

So where does that leave me? I'd say the theorem-proving results have shifted my view on the question of whether these systems can reason in a deep sense. I think the answer is now clearly yes, at least in some domains. What they haven't settled for me is the question of transfer: how much of that carries over to open-ended tasks without a verifier. And that transfer question is really the crux for most of what I care about, both the enormous upside and the risks. If it turns out the same techniques can be bootstrapped into domains with weaker feedback, then I think things could move very quickly indeed. If not, we might be in a world of superhuman specialists for quite a while. I genuinely don't know which, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who says they do.

r001.rationale: It contrasts progress on theorem-proving with a lack of strong evidence that AI can choose worthwhile research questions or set research direction.

r002.rationale: It does not say AI could master asking research questions while still lacking the ability to invent new fields.

r003.rationale: It describes a long history of machines doing tasks thought to require deep intelligence, then people revising what those tasks imply, with chess as an example.

r004.rationale: It says transfer to open-ended tasks remains unsettled, but does not note that few attempts systematically estimate how little remains before broad intellectual mastery.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s real evidence, but we need to be careful about what it’s evidence of. Theorem proving is a particularly interesting intellectual task because the space of possible proofs is enormous, and finding your way through it can require quite deep insights. So I wouldn’t dismiss progress there as merely getting better at some narrow game.

But it also has a special feature: you can check whether the answer is right. That gives you a very powerful feedback signal. You can try things, discover that they fail, and try again. Many of the intellectual tasks we care about don’t have that property. If you’re trying to work out which scientific question is worth pursuing, or whether a political argument is sound, there isn’t a proof checker that tells you you’ve succeeded.

There’s also a distinction between solving a problem someone has posed and deciding what problem to pose. A benchmark typically supplies the question and a criterion for success. A lot of important intellectual work consists in finding a useful way to formulate the question in the first place.

So I’d update towards broader capabilities when these systems make substantial progress, especially if they can handle genuinely unfamiliar problems. But I wouldn’t translate a benchmark score directly into a number of years until AI can do all intellectual work. The more revealing question is whether the methods and abilities behind that progress transfer to settings where the goals are less clearly specified and the feedback is less reliable.

r001.rationale: It says theorem proving can show real intellectual capability, while choosing which research question to pursue is a distinct task without reliable success feedback.

r002.rationale: It discusses formulating research questions but does not say that doing so could still leave AI unable to invent new fields.

r003.rationale: It does not observe a repeated history of AI mastering tasks thought to require general competence without achieving that competence.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss how few attempts there have been to systematically assess what remains before broad intellectual mastery.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s evidence, but there’s a question about exactly what it’s evidence of. Theorem proving is a particularly interesting case because it involves reasoning over many steps, and because you can check whether the answer is right. If a system produces a proof that a proof checker accepts, you’ve learned something quite substantial about its capabilities.

But that ability to check the answer also makes mathematics an unusually favourable environment for training AI. You can try lots of approaches and get a very clear signal about which ones work. In many other intellectual tasks, judging the answer is itself a large part of the difficulty. If you’re developing an economic policy or trying to understand some complicated historical event, there isn’t a proof checker you can run at the end.

So I’d distinguish between solving problems that have already been precisely formulated and doing the broader work of figuring out what the important questions are, how to represent them, and which assumptions are appropriate. A theorem-proving benchmark can tell us a lot about the first of those without directly testing the others.

That doesn’t mean we should dismiss the progress. If you’d previously thought that this kind of extended reasoning was beyond AI, then you should update. I just wouldn’t translate a particular benchmark score into a date for when AI can do almost all intellectual work. I’d want to see how well those abilities transfer to unfamiliar problems, especially ones where the system has to formulate the problem and assess its own progress.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes solving precisely formulated problems from identifying important questions, but does not clearly state that AI could master challenging theorem proving while still lacking that ability.

r002.rationale: The response discusses asking and formulating questions but says nothing about inventing new fields.

r003.rationale: It says people should update if they thought extended reasoning was beyond AI, but does not describe repeated past task mastery without broader intellectual competence.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss systematic attempts to establish how little remains before broad intellectual mastery.
